opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I find most useful is to stop thinking of it as "prompting" in some magical incantation sense and start thinking of it as briefing a very smart, very eager new colleague who has zero context on what you're doing. A lot of people write these terse little one-line instructions and then get frustrated when the model does something reasonable but not what they wanted. But if you handed that same one-liner to a talented intern on their first day, they'd also flounder.

So my go-to approach is to just write a lot. I'll explain the goal, why I care about it, what a good answer looks like, what failure modes I've seen before, and what I specifically *don't* want. Often I'll literally dictate it, just rambling into a voice-to-text tool for a few minutes, because it's much faster than typing and it naturally captures the context I'd otherwise leave out. The models are good at pulling the signal out of a messy brain dump.

The second thing is iteration. When it gets something wrong, rather than just saying "no, try again," I ask myself what context it was missing that would have made the right answer obvious, and I add that to the prompt. Over time you build up reusable prompts that encode a lot of your taste.

And a third trick: ask the model to help. Something like "here's what I'm trying to do, what questions would you need answered to do this well?" or "here's a prompt I wrote, how would you improve it?" It's surprisingly good at spotting where you've been ambiguous.

The underlying mindset shift is that these systems are now capable enough that the bottleneck is usually your communication, not their ability. If it's failing, the first hypothesis should be "I didn't explain this well," not "the model can't do this."

r001.rationale: The response recommends dictating a brain dump and says models can extract its signal, but it does not clearly say to have an LLM turn the dictation into a coherent prompt.

r002.rationale: It recommends using a failed output to identify missing context and adding that context to the prompt, but does not say to have the LLM revise the prompt for future use.

fable-5.1.text:
One thing I've found surprisingly effective is to just explain to the model why I want what I want. People tend to treat prompting like programming, where you issue terse commands and expect compliance. But these systems are trained on an enormous amount of human text, and they're much better at modelling a situation than at parsing a rulebook. So if I say "don't use bullet points," it'll often slip anyway. If I say "I'm going to paste this into an email to a colleague who finds bullet points patronising, so please write in flowing prose," it basically never slips, and it also makes a bunch of other sensible choices I didn't explicitly ask for, because it now understands the context it's operating in.

The related trick is giving it a few examples of exactly what good looks like. Models are extremely good at pattern matching. Three worked examples of the input-output pair you want will often do more than a page of carefully worded instructions, especially for things like tone or formatting that are hard to specify precisely in words.

And honestly, the meta-approach is to just iterate. Treat the first prompt as a draft. Look at where the output went wrong, ask yourself what a reasonable person could have misunderstood about your instruction, and fix that. You can even ask the model itself: "You did X when I wanted Y, what in my prompt made you do that?" It's often quite good at diagnosing the ambiguity. I think people underrate how much of prompting is just clear communication, the same skill you'd use delegating to a smart new colleague who doesn't yet know your context.

r001.rationale: The response recommends explaining the task’s context and giving examples, but does not describe turning rambling voice dictation into a coherent prompt.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking the model why it misunderstood an instruction, then having the user fix the prompt. It does not recommend having the model revise the prompt for future use.

astra-6.text:
I find it useful to think of it as giving instructions to a very capable person who’s missing a lot of context. You know what you mean, but that doesn’t mean the model knows what you mean. So be explicit about what you want, give examples of what a good answer looks like, and spell out the constraints that actually matter.

And then iterate. Try the prompt on a few different inputs and look at where it goes wrong. Often you’ll realise that there’s an ambiguity in what you asked for, or some assumption you never stated. Fixing that tends to be more useful than trying to find a magic phrase that makes the model obey.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing prompts and fixing ambiguities, but does not say to give the LLM feedback on an unsatisfactory output so it can revise the prompt for future use.

sol-6.1.text:
I find it useful to think of prompting as an empirical process. You have some behaviour you want, you write down instructions that you think describe it, and then you actually look at what the model does. And when it does something weird, you ask, “What was ambiguous here? What did I leave implicit?”

One thing that helps is giving examples. If I want a particular kind of answer, showing the model a couple of answers that capture what I mean can be much more effective than adding another paragraph of abstract instructions. And ideally you try it on a few different inputs, because getting the answer you wanted once doesn’t tell you very much about whether the instructions work reliably.

There’s also this surprisingly useful move of just being explicit about what you’re trying to achieve. Give it the context, explain what a good result looks like, and let it work out some of the details.
